question: How does a recipient determine the length of a message body in an HTTP/1.1 message?

claims.text: In rfc9112#6.3, a recipient determines the length of an HTTP/1.1 message body by applying the specified rules in order of precedence.

In rfc9112#6.3, any response to a HEAD request and any response with a 1xx, 204, or 304 status code is terminated by the first empty line after the header fields and therefore cannot contain a message body or trailer section.

In rfc9112#6.3, any 2xx response to a CONNECT request means the connection becomes a tunnel immediately after the empty line ending the header fields, and the client must ignore any Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding fields in that message.
In rfc9112#6.3, if a message contains both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding overrides Content-Length.

In rfc9112#6.3, an intermediary that forwards a message containing both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length must remove the received Content-Length field and process the Transfer-Encoding before forwarding the message downstream.

In rfc9112#6.3, if Transfer-Encoding is present and chunked is the final transfer coding, the message body length is determined by reading and decoding the chunked data until the transfer coding indicates completion.
In rfc9112#6.3, if Transfer-Encoding is present in a response and chunked is not the final transfer coding, the message body length is determined by reading the connection until the server closes it.

In rfc9112#6.3, if Transfer-Encoding is present in a request and chunked is not the final transfer coding, the message body length cannot be determined reliably and the server must respond with 400 Bad Request and close the connection.

In rfc9112#6.3, if a message has no Transfer-Encoding and has an invalid Content-Length, the message framing is invalid and the recipient must treat it as an unrecoverable error unless the field value is a comma-separated list whose values are all valid and identical.

In rfc9112#6.3, when an invalid Content-Length value can be parsed as a comma-separated list whose values are all valid and identical, the message is processed using that single value as the Content-Length value.
In rfc9112#6.3, if a valid Content-Length is present without Transfer-Encoding, its decimal value defines the expected message body length in octets.

In rfc9112#6.3, if the sender closes the connection or the recipient times out before the number of octets indicated by Content-Length is received, the recipient must consider the message incomplete and close the connection.
In rfc9112#6.3, if the message is a request and none of the preceding rules applies, the message body length is zero.
In rfc9112#6.3, if the message is otherwise a response without a declared message body length, the message body length is the number of octets received before the server closes the connection.

In rfc9112#6.3, request messages are never close-delimited because they are explicitly framed by length or transfer coding, and the absence of both means the request ends immediately after the header section.
